# (PART) Testing {-}

# Null Distributions {#null-distributions}

<div class="draft">Work in progress.</div>

## How Far Is Far Enough?

- In Chapter \@ref(standard-error-t), the ten scores were about 1 SE from 49 (t = 0.95) and nearly 4 SEs from 46 (t = 3.79)
- The second feels more convincing, but how far is far enough?
- To answer that we need to know what t-values look like when there is no real difference, when the population mean equals the comparison value
- "No real difference" is the **null hypothesis**. The spread of t-values when it's true is the **null distribution**
- We build it the way we built the sampling distribution in Chapter \@ref(sampling-distributions): take many samples and keep a result from each

<div class="summary-box">
sample -> group mean -> t-value -> repeat many times -> null distribution -> which values are rare?
</div>

<div class="note">
**What you need for this chapter**

- Chapters \@ref(sampling-distributions) and \@ref(standard-error-t)

## A World Where The Null Is True

- In real research we never know whether the null is true. In a simulation we can make it true on purpose
- A made-up question: are people called Steve taller than average? We build a world where they aren't
- Everyone's heights have a mean of 175 cm and an SD of 7 cm, and Steves' heights are exactly the same (made up, but realistic for adults)

```{r steve-world, fig.cap="Left: in this world, the heights of people called Steve (dashed) match everyone's heights (filled) exactly. Right: a random sample of 10 Steves from that world. The heights are made up but realistic.", fig.alt="Two panels with height in centimetres on the x-axis. On the left, a filled normal curve for everyone and a dashed curve for people called Steve lie exactly on top of each other, centred on a dotted line at 175. On the right, ten dots for a sample of Steves, with a dotted line at 175 and a solid orange line at the sample mean of 179, about 4 cm higher.", echo=FALSE}
set.seed(4)
steves <- tibble(
  height = rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7),
  y = 1:10,
  panel = "Our sample"
)

world <- tibble(height = seq(150, 200, by = 0.5)) |>
  mutate(density = dnorm(height, mean = 175, sd = 7), panel = "The world")

mean_lines <- tibble(
  panel = c("The world", "Our sample", "Our sample"),
  height = c(175, 175, mean(steves$height)),
  line = c("average", "average", "sample mean")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = world, aes(x = height, y = density, fill = "Everyone"),
            alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = world, aes(x = height, y = density,
                              colour = "People called Steve"),
            linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = steves, aes(x = height, y = y),
             size = 3, colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_vline(data = mean_lines, aes(xintercept = height, linetype = line),
             colour = c("grey20", "grey20", "#D55E00"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(panel, levels = c("The world", "Our sample")),
             scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c("Everyone" = "#467AAC")) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("People called Steve" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(NULL, values = c("average" = "dotted",
                                         "sample mean" = "solid")) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend(order = 1),
    colour = guide_legend(order = 2),
    linetype = guide_legend(
      order = 3, override.aes = list(colour = c("grey20", "#D55E00"))
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Height (cm)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 12),
        panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"))
```

```{r steve-world-code, ref.label="steve-world", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- Here the null is true: Steves are exactly average
- But this sample of 10 has a mean of `r round(mean(steves$height), 1)` cm, about `r round(mean(steves$height) - 175)` cm above average
- Nothing makes Steves taller in this world. The gap comes only from which Steves ended up in the sample, which is sampling noise
- A one-sample t-test compares the sample mean with 175. So the question is how big a gap noise alone can produce
- In R, `rnorm()` draws 10 Steves from the population, and `my_t_value()` compares them with 175:

```{r one-null-sample}
null_sample <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)
my_t_value(null_sample, comparison_value = 175)
```

- Run it a few times. The t-value changes every time, though nothing is going on
- Heights are in cm. t is the same comparison measured in standard errors, so t = 2 means the mean is two SEs above 175

1. Click **+1** a few times and watch each group's mean land in the histogram
2. Click **+10** and **+100**. Compare the spread of the means with the spread of individual heights
3. Tick **Expected shape** and compare **SD of the means** with **Formula SE**

- The same in R, as in Chapter \@ref(sampling-distributions): 1000 groups of 10, keeping each mean

```{r null-means}
set.seed(10)
null_means <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) my_mean(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)))
```

- The means are much tighter than individual heights: an SD of `r round(my_sd(null_means), 1)` cm against 7 cm
- That's the standard error from Chapter \@ref(standard-error-t), 7 / √10 = `r round(7 / sqrt(10), 2)` cm
- Some are still far from 175. The tallest group averaged `r round(max(null_means), 1)` cm and the shortest `r round(min(null_means), 1)` cm, all in a world where Steves are average

- Wrap those steps in a function that takes a sample size, a population mean and a population SD

  1. draw a sample with `rnorm()`
  2. work out t with `my_t_value()`, using the population mean as the comparison value
- Comparing with the population mean is what makes the null true

```{r my-null-t-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <-
  output <-
  return(output)
}

my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`sample_values` is `rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)`, and `output` is `my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-null-t-solution}
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <- rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  output <- my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)
  return(output)
}

my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
```
`r unhide()`

- The exercise file checks it against `t.test()` on the same random numbers, using `set.seed()`

## Many t-Values

- Run it 1000 times:

```{r null-ts}
set.seed(10)
null_ts <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7))
```

- This is the null distribution of t for samples of 10:

```{r null-histogram, fig.cap="1000 t-values from groups of 10 Steves in a world where the null hypothesis is true.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 simulated t-values centred on zero, with most between -2 and 2 and a few further out in both tails.", echo=FALSE}
ggplot(tibble(t = null_ts), aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, colour = "white", fill = "#467AAC") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count")
```

```{r null-histogram-code, ref.label="null-histogram", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- Each t is one group, measured in SEs rather than cm
- It's centred on 0, because on average the sample mean equals the population mean
- Most t-values are between about -2 and 2
- A few are further out in both directions, even though the null is true
- The shape doesn't depend on the population mean or SD, only on the sample size. Any 10 values from a normal population give the same null distribution, and the next chapter relies on this

- Which t-values are common and which are rare? The widget draws 1000 null t-values at a time
- The slider picks the rarest share, split across the two tails

<iframe class="demyst-widget" src="apps/rareness/embed.html" width="100%" height="480" title="Which t-values are rare interactive widget" style="border: 0;"></iframe>

1. Click **Regenerate** a few times. The details change but the shape stays
2. Move the slider. Orange marks the rarest values, and the sentence under the plot says where they start
3. How far from 0 do you go before only the rarest 5% are left? Is it the same after regenerating?

## Where Do The Rare Values Start?

- Put the t-values in order with `sort()`, smallest to largest
- The rarest 5% of 1000 is 50 values, 25 in each tail
  - the **lower cutoff** is the 26th smallest, with 25 below it
  - the **upper cutoff** is the 975th, with 25 above it
- Square brackets pick a value by position: `sorted_ts[1]` is the smallest, `sorted_ts[1000]` the largest

### Your Turn: Pick Them Out By Position

```{r cutoffs-by-position-exercise, eval=FALSE}
sorted_ts <- sort(null_ts)
lower <-
upper <-

c(lower = lower, upper = upper)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`lower` is `sorted_ts[26]`. Which position is `upper`?
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r cutoffs-by-position-solution}
sorted_ts <- sort(null_ts)
lower <- sorted_ts[26]
upper <- sorted_ts[975]

c(lower = lower, upper = upper)
```

### Your Turn: Write `my_cutoffs()`

- Positions 26 and 975 only work for 1000 values and 5%. A function handles any number of values and any share
- `alpha` is the share we mark as rare (`0.05` for the rarest 5%). The next chapter explains it properly
- Steps:
  1. sort the t-values
  2. count them with `length()`
  3. `k` is the number of values in each tail
  4. the lower cutoff is at position `k + 1`, the upper at `n - k`

```{r my-cutoffs-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <-
  n <-
  k <-
  lower <-
  upper <-
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs(null_ts)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`sorted` is `sort(null_ts)` and `n` is `length(sorted)`. `k` is `floor(n * alpha / 2)`, which gives 25 for 1000 values; `floor()` rounds down because positions are whole numbers. `lower` is `sorted[k + 1]` and `upper` is `sorted[n - k]`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-cutoffs-solution}
my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <- sort(null_ts)
  n <- length(sorted)
  k <- floor(n * alpha / 2)
  lower <- sorted[k + 1]
  upper <- sorted[n - k]
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs(null_ts)
```
`r unhide()`

- Same values as picking them out by position
- `alpha = 0.05` is a default, so we don't have to type it each time

### See The Rare Values

- Orange t-values are past the cutoffs, and the dashed lines are the cutoffs
- In the code, `|` means "or": `rare` is TRUE below the lower cutoff or above the upper one
- Try `alpha_choice` at 0.5, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01

```{r rare-plot, fig.cap="The null t-values, with the rarest 5% (alpha_choice = 0.05) in orange and dashed lines at the cutoffs.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 null t-values in blue, with the bars beyond about -2.3 and 2.3 coloured orange and dashed vertical lines at those two values."}
alpha_choice <- 0.05
rare_cutoffs <- my_cutoffs(null_ts, alpha = alpha_choice)

null_t_data <- tibble(t = null_ts) |>
  mutate(rare = t < rare_cutoffs[1] | t > rare_cutoffs[2])

ggplot(null_t_data, aes(x = t, fill = rare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_cutoffs, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#467AAC", "TRUE" = "#D55E00"),
                    guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count")
```

- At 0.05, exactly `r sum(null_t_data$rare)` of the 1000 are past the cutoffs, 25 in each tail, because that's how we chose them
- A smaller share moves the cutoffs outwards, so only t-values further from 0 count as rare
- R's `qt()` gives the cutoffs for the exact t distribution: `r round(qt(0.025, df = 9), 2)` and `r round(qt(0.975, df = 9), 2)` with 9 degrees of freedom. Ours are `r sprintf("%.2f", my_cutoffs(null_ts)[1])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", my_cutoffs(null_ts)[2])`, close but not identical, because a new `null_ts` would give slightly different cutoffs

## Rare, But Not Impossible

- Back to the Steves. If they're average, unusually tall or short groups of 10 are rare
- Of the 1000 group means, only `r sum(null_means > 180)` were above 180 cm and `r sum(null_means < 170)` below 170 cm
- The tallest 25 groups were all above `r round(sort(null_means)[975], 1)` cm
- A group that tall would make us wonder, but there's no believable reason for Steves to be taller, so a fluke is still the better explanation
- Compare a group exposed to a toxin while growing up that turns out unusually short. That result is just as rare, but a toxin affecting growth is believable, so "something is going on" beats a fluke
- 5% of null t-values are still past the cutoffs. Test 100 first names that are all truly average, and about 5 will look unusual from noise alone

# Null Distributions -------------------------------------------------------
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <- rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  output <- my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <- sort(null_ts)
  n <- length(sorted)
  k <- floor(n * alpha / 2)
  lower <- sorted[k + 1]
  upper <- sorted[n - k]
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}
```
